10.1002_adma.75640: Although electrochemical CO 2 ‐to‐CH 4 conversion offers a viable pathway to sustainable fuel synthesis, its efficiency is limited by the difficulty of balancing the availability of reactive hydrogen species for multistep CO 2 hydrogenation against the suppression of the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Here, we establish a spin‐selective catalytic strategy using Ag‐modified chiral Cu electrocatalysts to overcome this intrinsic trade‐off. Structural chirality in the Cu framework induces chirality‐induced spin selectivity, which disfavors spin‐singlet H 2 formation, thereby mitigating the HER and favoring productive hydrogen utilization toward CO 2 hydrogenation. Ag modification facilitates the supply of *CO intermediates on adjacent Cu sites. Thus, the chiral Ag/Cu catalyst selectively drives CO 2 reduction toward CH 4 , delivering a CH 4 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 67.0% at −0.7 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode while suppressing the HER. When coupled with perovskite‐based photoelectrochemical electrodes, the chiral catalyst enables unassisted solar‐driven CO 2 ‐to‐CH 4 conversion with an FE CH4 of 54.1% and a solar‐to‐fuel efficiency of 5.86%. These results suggest spin‐selective hydrogen utilization as an effective approach to selective hydrocarbon synthesis and bias‐free solar CO 2 ‐to‐fuel conversion.
10.1016_j.electacta.2026.148465: • Validation of electrodialysis process for desalinating real wastewater from WWTP with by high. • Success of electrodialysis process under complex operation in real scenario. • Validation of an electrodialysis scale-up from synthetic water in a pre-pilot system to real water in a pilot system at a WWTP. • Mitigation of Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ salt precipitation in the electrodialysis system through electrolyte optimization and operation control. Seawater intrusion in pipeline systems of coastal Spanish cities represents a major problem since current national regulations establish that the conductivity of discharge wastewater must be below 3 mS·cm -1 . The reuse for agricultural use is denied as well for the same reason. Electrodialysis (ED) is an energy-affordable membrane technology that desalinates moderate conductivity water without removing beneficial elements for plants. In this study, a pre-pilot and an in-situ pilot ED systems were successfully evaluated to test the capability of desalinate tertiary wastewater from Santa Pola’s wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). At pre-pilot scale, current efficiencies close to 90 % were achieved, and energy consumption between 0.42 and 1.34 kWh·m -3 . Scaling the process up to an in-situ pilot achieved current efficiencies above 60 % and an electric consumption between 0.15 and 0.34 kWh·m -3 , with water recovery above 80 %, treating a continuous flow rate of 600 L·h -1 . The wastewater conductivity was reduced from 4-7 mS·cm -1 (depending on the month of the year) to 2.5 mS·cm -1 . The ED pilot reactor is composed of 60 cells and an electrode area of 1000 cm 2 . It was demonstrated that appropriate wastewater pre-filtration and ultraviolet pretreatment is mandatory for the long-term viability of the ED process.
10.1038_s41467-026-70977-0: Electrolysis of CO 2 in molten salts promises efficient carbon capture, but the underlying reaction mechanisms remain incompletely understood, as research thus far has been limited by a lack of tools for operando investigations. Here, we use a high-temperature operando Raman spectroelectrochemical system to look for signatures of reaction intermediates and study the evolution of carbon structures over electrolysis time. The analysis reveals the existence of O 2 2− concurrently with the deposition of carbon on Au, W, Inconel, and Ni electrode materials, pointing to a common reaction mechanism with O 2 2− as an intermediate. Secondly, the G peak of the as-deposited carbon experiences a noticeable blue-shift as the material is cooled down and purified, suggesting either a growth in crystallite size even after the electrolysis is stopped or lithium deintercalation. Elucidating the cathodic carbon deposition mechanism could help create greater value-added products and increase the economic viability of carbon capture.
